name: Aaron Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can give me the public version and the private one. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In winter it's mostly feeding. We've got 250 suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves for beef, and they're in the sheds now, so I'm on the loader with silage and hay from seven till about eleven. Then it's bedding, checking for sick calves, fixing gates. I work for Mrs Okafor, who took the farm over from her dad, and in summer we make hay for ourselves and for about ten other farms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hay-making, easily. Racing the weather, three days of sun, everyone baling till midnight. What wears me out is that I'm still slow at the stock work compared to the others, I miss things a better stockman would spot. I use an AI app every day for grazing plans and the hay weather, and that helps cover my gaps. My partner Jess is a vet nurse, and we've got maybe a month of rent saved, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of a letdown, honestly. I was hoping it'd get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, it just isn't the miracle. At the mart I'd tell the older lads it's good for the weather and the paperwork, so try it. Online I'd share how I use it for grazing, because a few people asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a flop would be a bit of a shame for me, because the app's what makes me look better than I am. But it'd also mean nobody's coming for my job. Beef prices would still be up and down, and I'd still be on the lower end of the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the app. I'd push Mrs Okafor to let me take over the hay contracting side as my own little business, paying her for the kit. I'd try saving £100 a month by doing extra baling for neighbours on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app makes you look better than you are. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It spots patterns I'd miss, like which field's going to run out of grass first. Mrs Okafor's dad could tell by walking it. I can't yet. So the app is sort of my secret apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel bad about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather use what's there than pretend. But I know I need to actually learn it too, not just trust the phone.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still worth using, it just isn't a miracle. I'd tell the older farmers at the mart to try it for weather and paperwork, and share how I use it for grazing.
S0.think: A flop would be a shame for me, because the app makes me look better than I am. But it would mean nobody is coming for my job, though beef prices would still swing and my pay would stay low.
S0.do: Keeps using the grazing and weather app and asks his employer to let him run the hay contracting as his own small business. Tries to save £100 a month from weekend baling for neighbours.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit flat but okay.
S0.quote: So the app is sort of my secret apprenticeship.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron uses AI daily to make up for skills he hasn't built yet, and he's open about it. He's entrepreneurial even in a flat picture, aiming to run the hay contracting as his own business. He doesn't blame anyone and speaks about the market and prices as weather to be managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong but not a revolution. That's what I'd guess, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board early, because the people who learn the kit first will be the ones running it. At the young farmers I'd say it straight. Online I'd share what's working and what isn't, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the feeding goes to robots first, the self-driving feed wagons already exist. That's half my morning gone. But the hay contracting, the deals with neighbours, the fixing things, that lasts longer. So I'd shift towards that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd talk Mrs Okafor into trying a robot feeder and offer to set it up, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd buy a second-hand baler on finance, maybe £8,000 over three years, to grow the contracting. And I'd do a short welding course at the college, because things still break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: £8,000 on a month of savings. What does Jess think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm mad, and then she'd help me with the spreadsheet. If the baler earns its keep by year two, we're fine. If it doesn't, we're in trouble and I'd have to sell it at a loss. That's the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for retraining in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. The government should help, but I'm not going to sit and wait for it. If I can pay for a course myself, I will.

S1.say: I'd say get on board early, because the people who learn the kit first will be the ones running it. I'd say it straight at the young farmers and share honestly online what works and what doesn't.
S1.think: Feeding goes to robots first, which is half my morning gone. But the hay contracting, the deals with neighbours and the fixing last longer, so I'd shift towards those.
S1.do: Persuades his employer to try a robot feeder and sets it up himself. Buys a second-hand baler on finance, about £8,000 over three years, to grow his contracting, and takes a short welding course.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a little nervous about the loan.
S1.quote: She'd say I'm mad, and then she'd help me with the spreadsheet.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron is the most willing to take on debt of anyone in this set, even on a month of savings. He sees robots as taking the routine morning work and plans to move into the parts that involve dealing with people and fixing things. His partner acts as his reality check, which he seems to welcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. So the baler plan is a bad idea now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's be smart about it rather than angry. At the mart I'd tell people to sell their old kit before it's worth nothing. Online I'd share the practical stuff, what I'm doing and what I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years means no point in a loan or a baler, because the robot baler will be cheaper than me. I'd have one or two years of being the guy who sets up the robots for farms round here. After that, I've got no idea, and anyone who says they know is lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not buy the baler. I'd go to Mrs Okafor in the first week and say let me be the one who brings the robots in, and train me up. I'd offer the same to the other farms we make hay for, charging a fee to set up their machines. And Jess and I would save every penny, because once the setup work's done, there's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Racing, like hay-making in a thunderstorm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Jess's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks the animals still need a human, and the farmers would too. I'm less sure. If her job holds on even a year longer than mine, that's our cushion. We'd live on her wage and save mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the work dried up here, yes, without much drama. I'd go wherever the new jobs were. Jess would be harder to move, she loves her practice, but she's practical too.

S2.say: It's here, so let's be smart about it rather than angry. I'd tell people at the mart to sell old kit before it's worthless, and share online what I'm doing and what I'm not.
S2.think: Two years means no point in a loan or a baler, because a robot baler will be cheaper than me. I'd get a year or two setting up robots for local farms, and after that nobody knows.
S2.do: Drops the baler plan and asks his employer in the first week to let him bring the robots in. Charges other farms to set up their machines, and saves every penny while living on his partner's wage.
S2.feel: Anxious and racing, like hay-making in a thunderstorm.
S2.quote: After that, I've got no idea, and anyone who says they know is lying.
S2.fieldNote: Faced with two years, Aaron drops his investment plan at once, which shows good sense under pressure. He moves fast to become the person who installs the machines, but he's clear that this is only a short bridge. He'd move without much fuss, unlike many others in this set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something that lasts a while. I'd tell the other young farmers to learn the machines now. Online I'd post a how-to, because people will need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent run. I could have a small business setting up and fixing farm robots for three or four years. That might pay off Jess's car, and maybe a deposit on a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do a robotics maintenance course and get the dealer's training. I'd skip the baler, but buy a van and tools on a small loan, about £5,000. By year two I'd have a list of ten or fifteen farms I look after, and by year four I'd be thinking about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a good way. Like the night before harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip the baler but take a loan for a van. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The baler only earns while people still make hay the old way. The van earns while there are machines to fix, which lasts longer. Same risk, better bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Mrs Okafor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want her to keep the farm. She's worked her whole life for it. If I can set up the robots cheap for her, that's my way of paying her back for taking a chance on me.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to build something that lasts a while. I'd tell other young farmers to learn the machines now and post a how-to online, because people will need it.
S3.think: Five years is a decent run: three or four years of a small business setting up and fixing farm robots. That might pay off my partner's car and maybe a house deposit.
S3.do: Takes a robotics maintenance course and dealer training in year one, then buys a van and tools on a £5,000 loan instead of the baler. Builds a list of ten to fifteen client farms by year two.
S3.feel: Anxious in a good way, like the night before harvest.
S3.quote: The van earns while there are machines to fix, which lasts longer. Same risk, better bet.
S3.fieldNote: Aaron thinks like a small business owner, weighing which investment pays for longest. With five years he builds a real bridge, and he's loyal to his employer, wanting to help her keep the farm. He accepts the risk calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper career, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good amount of time if you use it. I'd tell people to stop arguing about whether it's coming and start planning. Online I'd be the hopeful one, sharing what's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years could set me up. I could build a farm robotics business, hire a couple of people and have a decent pot by 37. But I'd be thinking: what's the plan for after 2036? Because the robots fixing robots bit comes eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First two years: the baler and the hay contracting, because it pays now. Years three to five: robotics training and a van, switching the business over. By year eight I'd want savings of at least a year, so whatever happens in 2036, Jess and I can ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. Ten years is a lot of time to be clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, around year four or five. Jess wants two. With ten years' warning I'd feel okay about it, because I'd know roughly what's coming. With two years I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to people who don't move as fast as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I worry about them. Some of the older stockmen, the ones who never touched a phone. I'd want the government to look after them, because the market won't.

S4.say: Ten years is a good amount of time if you use it. I'd tell people to stop arguing about whether it's coming and start planning, and be the hopeful one online.
S4.think: Ten years could set me up with a farm robotics business, a couple of staff and a decent pot by 37. But I'd be thinking about after 2036, because robots fixing robots comes eventually.
S4.do: Runs the baler and hay contracting for two years, then switches to robotics training and a van in years three to five. Aims for a year of savings by year eight and plans children around year four or five.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with plenty of time to be clever.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lot of time to be clever.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Aaron lays out a staged plan that runs from his current business to a new one, ending with a long cushion. He'd start a family with this much warning but not with two years. Though usually pragmatic about markets, he wants the government to protect slower movers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, I'd scramble, but for Jess and me together. Two years is no time to build a cushion. What would help is cheap, quick courses in robot setup and repair, and a safety net for people like the old stockmen who won't make the jump.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'd own the robots on farms like Mrs Okafor's. If it's the big dealers on subscription, the farmers lose too. I'd want it to be the farmers.

headlineQuote: Two years means no point in a loan or a baler, because the robot baler will be cheaper than me.
portrait: Aaron Torres is a 27-year-old junior worker on a 250-cow beef and hay farm, who uses an AI app every day to cover skills he's still learning. He lives with his partner Jess, a vet nurse, on about a month of savings. He thinks like a small business owner and is willing to borrow to grow his hay contracting, with Jess as his reality check. In the AGI pictures he quickly switches to setting up and fixing farm robots, though he sees it as a short bridge if the change comes in two years. With ten years he plans a staged business, a long cushion and children, while wanting the government to protect slower movers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is no time for him and Jess to build a cushion together.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick courses in robot setup and repair, and a safety net for older workers who won't make the jump.
